transfer.stem: Which set of notes keeps the container requirement, the role of a model and the stopping condition?
transfer.passage:
Models and observation
Our lesson used models to discuss matter and its changes of state. Ice was a solid form of water. A separate picture compared an ice cube with liquid water; it did not give temperatures or melting times. An instruction told us to pour a liquid into a labelled container. It did not identify the liquid or give its volume. We also learned that a gas can spread to fill its container. This did not say that every container was full of gas at that moment.
A model could help us picture an atom. It was a representation, not an exact photograph. Another diagram represented one water molecule. A separate composition exercise supplied this rule: one water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. The symbols in that exercise did not show actual sizes, distances or angles.
We looked at a plant cell through a microscope. The record gave no magnification or cell-structure findings. Another instruction told us to adjust the microscope until the image was clear. The condition was a clear image, not an invented one-minute limit.

options.text: Use an unlabelled container; a model is an exact photograph; stop while the image is blurred.
Use a labelled container; a model helps us picture an atom; stop when the image is clear.
Use a labelled container; one water molecule is one atom; stop when the image is clear.
Use a labelled container; a model helps us picture an atom; always stop after one minute.

answer.display: Use a labelled container; a model helps us picture an atom; stop when the image is clear.
